extracted.intended_audience: marketers, PR professionals, communicators, and anyone seeking to persuade an audience
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Dr. Robert Cialdini’s principles of persuasion to crafting messages (e.g., press releases, marketing copy, or influence attempts) so they more reliably elicit agreement or desired behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: People are obliged to give back to others the form of a behavior, gift, or service that they have received first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be the first to give; make the gift or favor personalized and unexpected. Examples: a single mint given with the bill increased tips ~3%; two mints produced a 14% increase; a single mint given plus a pause and a personal comment (“For you nice people, here’s an extra mint”) produced a 23% increase. Tactics for messaging: offer helpful free content, useful samples, favors or concessions before asking for the action. Emphasize genuine generosity rather than obvious manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: People want more of those things they can have less of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight uniqueness and what is at stake — explicitly point out what audiences stand to lose if they don't act. Example: British Airways Concorde announcement created demand by making the product scarce even though nothing about the product changed. Messaging tactics: call out limited availability, unique features, deadlines, or diminishing opportunity; explain losses or trade-offs from inaction rather than only listing benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: People follow the lead of credible, knowledgeable experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal credible expertise before making the influence appeal. Tactics include displaying credentials (e.g., diplomas), using uniforms/visual cues, or arranging third‑party introductions that name and validate expertise. Example: physiotherapists with diplomas get more compliance; reception staff who mention colleagues’ credentials increased appointments by 20% and signed contracts by 15%. Use endorsements, expert quotes, titles, or other signals that communicate competence; where possible have others introduce or recommend you to preserve modesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: People like to be consistent with the things they have previously said or done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elicit small, voluntary, active, public commitments first, ideally in writing; then request larger actions that are consistent with those commitments. Example: asking homeowners to place a small postcard in a window increased willingness to erect an unsightly billboard by 400%; asking patients to write appointment details reduced missed appointments by 18%. Tactics: design staged commitments (micro-commitments), use public or written confirmations, and highlight previous stated positions to prompt consistent behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer to say yes to those that they like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase similarity, give sincere compliments, and emphasize cooperation toward mutual goals. Example: negotiation groups that exchanged personal information and found similarities reached agreement 90% of the time (versus 55%) and produced outcomes worth ~18% more to both sides. Tactics for communications: find and highlight common ground, use personable humanizing details, and offer genuine praise or collaborative framing before making the ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially when they are uncertain, people look to the actions and behaviors of others to determine their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of comparable others’ behaviors (specific, honest statistics perform better than generic appeals). Example: standard towel‑reuse environmental messages produced ~35% compliance; adding that 75% of similar guests reuse towels increased reuse by 26% (and wording that emphasized comparable previous guests raised it 33%). Tactics: include truthful, concrete prevalence numbers, testimonials from similar people, case usage rates, and peer behaviors — especially effective when audience is uncertain or the referent is similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A seventh principle identifying shared identity, kinship, or belonging as a driver of influence (listed as one of the universals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists unity among the universals but provides no extended examples beyond naming it. In practice, tactics aligned with unity emphasize shared group identity, family/similarity ties, or us-vs-them framing to leverage a sense of belonging when requesting compliance; ensure ethical use and avoid divisive manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical application of persuasion principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding these shortcuts and employing them in an ethical manner can significantly increase the chances that someone will be persuaded by your request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly emphasizes ethical, costless implementation — use principles to make better, honest offers rather than to deceive. Guidance: favor transparent, honest signals (accurate social proof, legitimate scarcity, truthful credentials), avoid coercive or deceptive variants, and design interventions that respect recipients’ interests.
